es.summary: Dolor muscular en piernas que aparece al caminar y desaparece con el reposo, causado por flujo sanguíneo insuficiente por enfermedad arterial periférica.
key_points: Dolor se inicia con el ejercicio y se alivia al detenerse
Frecuente en mayores de 55 años, fumadores y diabéticos
Se asocia a disminución del índice tobillo‑brazo (ABI < 0.9)
Puede progresar a isquemia crítica y ulceración
El tratamiento combina cambios de estilo de vida, fármacos y ejercicio supervisado

pathophysiology: Aterosclerosis reduce el diámetro de arterias periféricas
Disminuye el flujo sanguíneo distal durante la actividad muscular
El metabolismo muscular genera ácido láctico → dolor y fatiga
Al reposo, la perfusión se restablece y el dolor desaparece
signs_symptoms: Dolor, ardor o calambres en pantorrilla, muslo o glúteos al caminar
Alivio del dolor al detener la marcha < 5 min
Piel fría y pálida distal al ejercicio
Marcha con cojera para evitar el dolor
diagnostics: Doppler arterial o ecografía duplex muestra flujo reducido
Angiografía por TC o MR para planificación quirúrgica
Perfil lipídico: colesterol total, LDL, HDL, triglicéridos
Glucosa en ayunas > 126 mg/dL sugiere diabetes
treatment: Cese total del tabaquismo y control glucémico
Cilostazol 100 mg cada 12 h para mejorar perfusión
Revascularización (angioplastia o bypass) si ABI < 0.4 o isquemia crítica
complications: Úlceras o gangrena por isquemia crónica
Disminución de la calidad de vida y movilidad
Mayor riesgo de eventos cardiovasculares (infarto, ACV)
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor antes, durante y después del ejercicio (escala 0‑10)
Monitorear pulsos pedales y temperatura de la piel
Registrar ABI y cambios en la marcha
Promover programa de caminata progresiva y registrar distancia recorrida
Administrar aspirina y estatina según orden y observar efectos adversos
patient_teaching: Explicar que el dolor es señal de flujo insuficiente y que el reposo al inicio es normal
Enseñar técnica de caminata: 5 min marcha, 1 min descanso, repetir hasta 30 min
Instruir sobre cese del tabaco y control de glucosa y colesterol
Mostrar cómo inspeccionar pies diariamente para detectar lesiones

related_to: Debilidad de los músculos de la pierna
evidenced_by: Dolor en pantorrilla al caminar 50 m
Disminución de la distancia de marcha
outcomes: Capacidad para caminar 200 m sin dolor (Escala de dolor ≤ 2)
Participación en programa de ejercicio 3 veces/semana

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de dolor antes y después de cada sesión de caminata
interventions.rationale: Permite ajustar la intensidad del ejercicio y prevenir sobrecarga

interventions.action: Planificar programa de caminata progresiva con intervalos de descanso
interventions.rationale: Mejora la perfusión muscular y aumenta la tolerancia al ejercicio

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de autocontrol del dolor (respiración profunda, cambio de postura)
interventions.rationale: Reduce la percepción de dolor y favorece la adherencia

interventions.action: Monitorear pulsos pedales y temperatura cutánea durante la actividad
interventions.rationale: Detecta signos tempranos de isquemia y permite intervención inmediata

interventions.action: Coordinar con fisioterapeuta para entrenamiento de resistencia y flexibilidad
interventions.rationale: Optimiza la capacidad funcional y previene la pérdida muscular

en.summary: Muscle pain in the legs that appears when walking and disappears with rest, caused by insufficient blood flow due to peripheral arterial disease.
key_points: Pain starts with exercise and is relieved when stopping
Common in people over 55, smokers, and diabetics
Associated with a decreased ankle‑brachial index (ABI < 0.9)
Can progress to critical ischemia and ulceration
Treatment combines lifestyle changes, medications, and supervised exercise

pathophysiology: Reduces distal blood flow during muscle activity
Muscle metabolism produces lactic acid → pain and fatigue
At rest, perfusion is restored and pain resolves
signs_symptoms: Pain, burning, or cramps in calf, thigh, or gluteal region when walking
Pain relief within < 5 minutes of stopping
Cold and pale skin distal to exercise
Gait with limping to avoid pain
diagnostics: Ankle‑brachial index (ABI) < 0.9 confirms peripheral arterial disease
Arterial Doppler or duplex ultrasound shows reduced flow
CT or MR angiography for surgical planning
Lipid profile: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides
treatment: Complete smoking cessation and glucose control
Cilostazol 100 mg every 12 hours to improve perfusion
Revascularization (angioplasty or bypass) if ABI < 0.4 or critical ischemia
complications: Ulcers or gangrene from chronic ischemia
Reduced quality of life and mobility
Increased risk of cardiovascular events (MI, stroke)
nursing_care: Assess pain before, during, and after exercise (0‑10 scale)
Monitor pedal pulses and skin temperature
Promote progressive walking program and record distance walked
Administer aspirin and statin as ordered and monitor for adverse effects
patient_teaching: Explain that pain signals insufficient flow and that rest at onset is normal
Teach walking technique: 5 min walk, 1 min rest, repeat until 30 min
Instruct on smoking cessation and control of glucose and cholesterol
Show how to inspect feet daily for injuries

evidenced_by: Limiting gait when attempting to walk
outcomes: Ability to walk 200 m without pain (pain scale ≤ 2)

interventions.action: Assess pain level before and after each walking session
interventions.rationale: Allows adjustment of exercise intensity and prevents overload

interventions.action: Plan progressive walking program with rest intervals
interventions.rationale: Improves muscle perfusion and increases exercise tolerance

interventions.action: Teach patient self‑management of pain (deep breathing, posture change)
interventions.rationale: Reduces pain perception and promotes adherence

interventions.action: Monitor pedal pulses and skin temperature during activity
interventions.rationale: Detects early signs of ischemia and allows immediate intervention

interventions.action: Coordinate with physical therapist for resistance and flexibility training
interventions.rationale: Optimizes functional capacity and prevents muscle loss

sources.name: Clinical Nursing Skills: Peripheral Vascular System

key_points.0.quote: A primary symptom of peripheral vascular disease is intermittent claudication , a cramp-like muscle pain, burning sensation, or extreme fatigue in the calf, thigh, or buttocks that is induced by exercise and relieved by rest.

key_points.3.quote: Chronic, or advanced, insufficiency can result in damage to the tissue of the extremities, including ulceration and gangrene.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: A primary symptom of peripheral vascular disease is intermittent claudication , a cramp-like muscle pain, burning sensation, or extreme fatigue in the calf, thigh, or buttocks that is induced by exercise and relieved by rest.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: The term arteriosclerosis encompasses the other reasons for the stiffening, which could include inflammation or smoking.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Heart failure, hypertension, and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are all disorders that must be accurately diagnosed to properly treat and alleviate edema.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: A primary symptom of peripheral vascular disease is intermittent claudication , a cramp-like muscle pain, burning sensation, or extreme fatigue in the calf, thigh, or buttocks that is induced by exercise and relieved by rest.

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: On assessment, the affected limb may feel cold to touch, pulses may be weak, and the skin will exhibit color changes such as pallor or decreased capillary refill due to insufficient blood getting to the limbs from arterial insufficiency.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: However, as the disease progresses, pain occurs when walking shorter distances and can cause a limp.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: A patient with suspected peripheral vascular disease will first undergo noninvasive imaging with an ultrasound to visualize flow in the vessels.

sections.complications.0.quote: Chronic, or advanced, insufficiency can result in damage to the tissue of the extremities, including ulceration and gangrene.

sections.complications.3.quote: Continuous blockage of arteries leads to obstruction of blood to vital organs, such as the heart, resulting in ischemia , which increases the risk of myocardial infarction.

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: Other interventions may include observing for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) , assessing popliteal and pedal pulses, assisting with position changes, and administering anticoagulants and pain medication as ordered.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: It could be intermittent claudication, which is pain caused by too little blood flow to muscles during exercise, such as walking.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Patients are encouraged to avoid high-cholesterol foods and stop smoking to prevent further vasoconstriction.
